headline: Two easy, low-HR days follow the week's hard tempo — recovery is being taken, and easy-run HR keeps trending down.
confidence_reasons: Multiple data sources active in last 3 days
summary:
The two most recent runs sit clearly in easy territory — relaxed paces, low heart rates, modest loads — which reads as deliberate recovery after the sharper tempo effort earlier in the week. That contrast is exactly what you want to see: the ability to run genuinely easy when the session calls for it, rather than grinding every day at the same moderate intensity. The lower easy-run HR on comparable efforts continues the aerobic-efficiency trend that's been holding for a couple of weeks now, so nothing here suggests fatigue accumulating.

Volume is essentially flat block-on-block, which at four weeks out from a nine-day self-supported crossing is a reasonable place to be — the base is durable and strength frequency has stepped up rather than eased. The gap that remains is specificity: the running is still general aerobic work, without the pack-loading, back-to-back durability, or sustained climbing that the border-mountain section will demand. That's the thing worth converting base into over the next few weeks, not more raw mileage.
watch_items: Whether the next quality session returns at a controlled HR, confirming these two easy days did their recovery job.
Whether pack-loaded or back-to-back running starts appearing, given the crossing's self-supported demands are now inside a month.
Whether per-run elevation begins climbing to rehearse the sustained up- and downhill of the border section.
Sleep has stayed erratic across tracked nights — worth watching whether it steadies as the event approaches, since accumulated recovery will matter more once specific durability work ramps.

evidence_items.text: ▼ Easy-run HR averaging 142 bpm vs 155 bpm prior period (comparable-effort runs, 8 vs 7 runs)
▼ 4-week volume 126 km vs 133 km prior block (-5%)
